name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q01 - Sequence of water movement through root layers

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological sequence for the movement of water from the soil into the root vascular cylinder:

(i) Diversion of water into the symplast at the endodermis due to the Casparian strip
(ii) Absorption of water along with mineral solutes by root hairs
(iii) Entry of water into non-living xylem vessels and tracheids
(iv) Movement of water through loosely packed cortical cells predominantly via the apoplast

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water absorbed from the soil travels radially across the root tissues to reach the xylem conduits, transitioning from apoplastic to symplastic flow at the endodermis.

Step 2: Sequential Evaluation
1. Water and mineral solutes are first absorbed from the soil by thin-walled root hairs (ii).
2. Next, most of the water flows inward through the loosely packed cortical cells via the apoplast pathway, as they offer no resistance (iv).
3. At the endodermis, the water-impervious suberised Casparian strip blocks apoplastic movement, forcing water across the plasma membrane into the symplast (i).
4. Finally, after crossing the endodermis and pericycle, water enters directly into the xylem vessels and tracheids (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence of water movement from soil to xylem is: absorption by root hairs \(\rightarrow\) apoplastic flow through cortex \(\rightarrow\) symplastic diversion at the endodermis \(\rightarrow\) entry into xylem vessels and tracheids, which corresponds to (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q02 - Sequence of stomatal opening and transpiration pull

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct logical sequence during stomatal opening and transpiration-driven water movement in a leaf:

(i) Thin outer walls of guard cells bulge out and force the thick inner walls into a crescent shape
(ii) Increase in turgidity within the two guard cells flanking the stomatal aperture
(iii) Pulling of water, molecule by molecule, into the leaf parenchyma cells from the xylem
(iv) Diffusion of water vapour from the substomatal cavity through the open stoma into the surrounding air

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stomatal opening is driven by guard cell turgidity, which permits evaporative water loss that subsequently generates the transpirational pull transmitted to the leaf xylem.

Step 2: Sequential Evaluation
1. First, turgidity increases within the two guard cells flanking the stomatal pore (ii).
2. This turgor pressure causes the thin outer walls to bulge outward, pulling the thick, elastic inner walls into a crescent shape and opening the stoma (i).
3. Once the stoma opens, water vapour diffuses from the higher concentration in the substomatal cavity and intercellular spaces into the drier surrounding air (iv).
4. Because the thin film of water over the leaf cells is continuous, this evaporation pulls water, molecule by molecule, into the leaf parenchyma from the xylem (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological order of events is: increase in guard cell turgidity \(\rightarrow\) bulging of outer walls to open the stoma \(\rightarrow\) diffusion of water vapour into surrounding air \(\rightarrow\) pulling of water from the xylem, which corresponds to (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q03 - Sequence of events in pressure flow hypothesis

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps of the pressure flow hypothesis for phloem translocation in the correct sequence from source to sink:

(i) Build-up of hydrostatic pressure drives mass flow of phloem sap toward regions of lower pressure
(ii) Active unloading of sucrose at the sink reduces osmotic pressure, causing water to exit the phloem
(iii) Active loading of sucrose into companion cells and sieve tube cells creates a hypertonic condition at the source
(iv) Water from the adjacent xylem moves into the phloem at the source by osmosis

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the pressure flow (mass flow) hypothesis, sugars move through phloem sieve tubes along a hydrostatic pressure gradient established by active loading at the source and active unloading at the sink.

Step 2: Sequential Evaluation
1. At the source, sucrose is actively transported into companion cells and then into living sieve tube cells, producing a hypertonic condition in the phloem (iii).
2. In response to this lowered water potential, water from the adjacent xylem enters the phloem sieve tube by osmosis (iv).
3. As osmotic and hydrostatic pressure builds up inside the sieve tube at the source, mass flow begins, pushing the sap toward regions of lower pressure at the sink (i).
4. At the sink, sucrose is actively transported out of the phloem into sink cells, reducing osmotic pressure and causing water to move out of the phloem back toward the xylem (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence from source to sink is: active loading of sucrose at source \(\rightarrow\) osmotic entry of water from xylem \(\rightarrow\) pressure-driven mass flow of sap \(\rightarrow\) active unloading at sink and exit of water, which corresponds to (iii) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (ii).
